pages.c22-p01: Describe what presentation software is used for and explain why a presentation must suit its audience and purpose
pages.c22-p02: Plan a presentation using a storyboard before building it
pages.c22-p03: Identify the main parts of the PowerPoint window and use slide layouts, placeholders and views
pages.c22-p04: Apply good slide design: the 6x6 guideline, contrast, readable fonts, consistency, design themes and the Slide Master
pages.c22-p05: Explain copyright, ownership, intellectual property and licensing (including Creative Commons), credit sources correctly, and use AI-generated images honestly
pages.c22-p06: Use charts, tables and SmartArt to present information clearly
pages.c22-p07: Use transitions and animations sensibly, choosing effects, order and timing to support the message
pages.c22-p08: Create hyperlinks and action buttons to build non-linear presentations such as quizzes and kiosk displays
pages.c22-p09: Apply accessibility guidelines and international standards (WCAG) to a presentation using alt text, contrast, colour-blind friendly colours, readable font sizes and the Accessibility Checker
pages.c22-p10: Use speaker notes, rehearse timings and Presenter View, and apply good speaking skills to deliver a presentation
pages.c22-p11: Evaluate a presentation against success criteria, using peer feedback, and refine it to improve usability

q.q: What is presentation software mainly used for?
o: Carrying out calculations on a grid of cells
Showing information as a series of slides
Editing the pixels of a photograph
q.why: Presentation software such as PowerPoint shows information slide by slide, usually to support a speaker.

q.q: In presentation planning, what does the word audience mean?
o: The people who will watch or use it
The room where it is shown
q.why: The audience is the people watching; what it should achieve is the purpose.

q.q: A looping slideshow on the TV in school reception shows this week's events. What is its main purpose?
o: To entertain at a quiz night
q.why: It displays notices to passers-by, so it informs and advertises rather than persuading.

q.q: Orla gives a talk on Lough Erne to a P3 class and to her Year 9 class. What should change most between the two versions?
o: The amount of text and the language used
The software used to make it
q.why: The audience changes how much text, how simple the words and which pictures are suitable.

q.q: Which of these is the best example of analysing user needs before building a presentation?
o: Picking the most colourful design theme first
Adding as many animations as possible
Asking a few audience members what they want to know
Copying a presentation made by another class
q.why: User-centred design starts by finding out what the users actually need, ideally by asking them.

q.q: Which is a communication convention most audiences expect at the end of a presentation?
o: A slide of animated clip art
A sources slide and a chance to ask questions
A list of every font you used
A blank slide with no content
q.why: Conventions include a title slide, a conclusion, a chance for questions and a sources slide.

q.q: Which opening line suits a formal presentation to a local business asking for sponsorship?
o: Right lads, let's get this started then
Good afternoon, and thank you for meeting us today
Hiya everyone, hope u r all ok
So, erm, this is our thing about rugby
q.why: A formal audience expects polite, clear language with no slang or text-speak.

q.q: Why is a presentation not the same as a written report?
o: The reader always controls the pace
It shows key points that support a speaker
It cannot include pictures or charts
It always contains more detail than a report
q.why: Slides show key points while the speaker explains; a report is read on its own with full detail.

q.q: Ciara is making an informal quiz for her friends. Which choice is still a mistake?
o: Using a bright, fun colour scheme
Adding a joke on the title slide
q.why: Informal tone is fine, but images must still be used legally and credited.

q.q: What is a storyboard?
o: A slide that tells a story with pictures
A plan of every slide made before building
A list of the transitions used
q.why: A storyboard is the plan, sketched before you open PowerPoint.

q.q: Which item belongs on a storyboard for each slide?
o: The name of the printer to use
The final file size in megabytes
The number of times it was saved
q.why: A storyboard notes the source of every image so it can be credited and checked.

q.q: What is the main benefit of storyboarding before building?
o: Problems are fixed on paper, saving time
It removes the need to rehearse
The slides will load more quickly
PowerPoint will add the content for you
q.why: It is quicker to change a plan than to rebuild finished slides.

q.q: A presentation that always runs slide 1, 2, 3, 4 in a fixed order is called…
q.why: Linear means one slide after another in a fixed order.

q.q: What extra detail does a storyboard for a non-linear quiz need?
o: A different theme for every slide
Arrows showing where each button leads
The exact time each slide will show
Speaker notes written word for word
q.why: Non-linear presentations need the links planned, usually as arrows between slides.

q.q: Which order of stages is the most sensible?
q.why: Decide audience and purpose, research, plan, then build and test.

q.q: Making a presentation follows which development cycle?
q.why: Like apps and websites, presentations go through planning, development, testing and refinement.

q.q: Which is the best way to write the text on a storyboard?
o: A photograph of each finished slide
q.why: A storyboard is a plan, so keywords and sketches are enough as long as it is complete.

q.q: What is the ribbon in PowerPoint?
o: The strip of tabbed tools across the top
The bar showing the slide number
The area under the slide for notes
The list of slide thumbnails on the left
q.why: The ribbon holds the tools, grouped into tabs such as Home and Insert.

q.q: Where do you type notes that only the presenter will see?
o: In the notes pane under the slide
In a text box on the slide
q.why: The notes pane holds speaker notes; the audience does not see them.

q.q: A dotted box saying Click to add title is called a…
q.why: Placeholders are the dotted boxes on a slide layout.

q.q: Which tab holds the Pictures, Table, Chart and SmartArt buttons?
q.why: The Insert tab adds new objects to a slide.

q.q: Which layout gives two side-by-side boxes, each with its own heading?
q.why: The Comparison layout has two content areas with a heading over each.

q.q: Which key starts the slide show from the slide you are working on?
q.why: F5 starts from the beginning; Shift + F5 starts from the current slide.

q.q: Which view shows all slides as tiles but does not let you edit their content?
q.why: Slide Sorter is for reordering, hiding and duplicating, not editing content.

q.q: Why should you use the title placeholder instead of drawing your own text box for a title?
o: It makes the file size much smaller
Screen readers use it to name the slide
Text boxes cannot be made bold
q.why: PowerPoint and screen readers recognise the title placeholder as the slide's title.

q.q: Aoibhinn changes an existing slide from Title and Content to Two Content. Which button does she use?
q.why: Home > Layout changes the layout of the selected slide.

q.q: What does the 6x6 guideline recommend?
o: Six seconds per slide for six minutes
Six slides with six pictures on each
About six bullets with about six words each
Six fonts in six different colours
q.why: It limits text so the audience listens instead of reading.

q.q: Which text and background pair has the poorest contrast?
o: Yellow text on a white background
Black text on a white background
Navy text on a cream background
White text on a navy background
q.why: Yellow on white has very low contrast and is hard to read.

q.q: Which font is the best choice for body text on a slide?
o: A plain sans-serif font such as Arial
A different decorative font per slide
Tiny text in capital letters only
q.why: Plain sans-serif fonts such as Arial, Calibri or Verdana are clear and readable.

q.q: A common guideline for the smallest body text size on a slide is about…
q.why: Around 24 point or more is readable from the back of a room.

q.q: Erin wants the school crest in the same corner of all 15 slides. What is the best method?
o: Paste it onto each slide separately
Add it once to the Slide Master
Add it to the speaker notes
Insert it as a transition effect
q.why: Anything on the Slide Master appears on every slide that uses it and can be changed once.

q.q: How do you open the Slide Master?
q.why: The Slide Master is on the View tab; click Close Master View to return.

q.q: What does applying a design theme do?
o: Adds alt text to every picture
Gives every slide matching colours and fonts
Checks the spelling on every slide
q.why: A theme applies a matching set of colours, fonts and backgrounds to all slides.

q.q: Rory's slide has a 50-word sentence about the Ulster Grand Prix. What is the best fix?
o: Make the font smaller so it all fits
Change the background to a photo
Add an animation to the whole sentence
Cut it to short points and put detail in the notes
q.why: Use keywords on the slide and move the detail into the speaker notes.

q.q: Which is the best reason to keep the same theme and transition on every slide?
o: It looks consistent and keeps focus on the content
It stops anyone else editing the file
PowerPoint will not save mixed themes
It makes the slides load faster
q.why: Consistency looks professional and avoids distracting the audience.

q.q: When does a photographer in the UK own the copyright of a photo?
o: Only after registering it with the government
Only once it has been sold
Automatically, as soon as it is taken
Only if it shows the copyright symbol
q.why: UK copyright is automatic; no registration or symbol is needed.

q.q: Which UK law protects copyright?
q.why: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 is the main UK copyright law.

q.q: For most works, how long does UK copyright last?
o: Ten years from when it was made
q.why: For most works copyright lasts for the creator's life plus 70 years.

q.q: Which of these is intellectual property?
o: A computer mouse in the lab
A bus that runs to Belfast
q.why: Intellectual property is something created with the mind, such as a song, photo or design.

q.q: What does a licence for an image tell you?
o: How to add alt text to it
What you may and may not do with it
How many pixels the image has
q.why: A licence is the owner's permission and its conditions.

q.q: What does the BY part of a Creative Commons licence require?
o: Do not make money from it
Share changes under the same licence
q.why: BY means attribution: you must credit the creator.

q.q: Darragh wants to crop a photo licensed CC BY-ND. What is the problem?
o: BY means he cannot use it at all
BY means he must pay the creator
ND means he must not credit it
ND means he must not change it
q.why: No Derivatives means no changes, and cropping is a change.

q.q: A CC BY-NC image is used on a poster that will be sold at the school fair. Is this allowed?
o: Yes, as long as it is cropped first
No, NC means non-commercial use only
No, BY means it cannot be printed
q.why: NC forbids using the work to make money.

q.q: What do the letters TASL stand for when crediting an image?
q.why: A good credit gives the Title, Author, Source and Licence.

q.q: Why is "I found it on Google Images" not permission to use a picture?
o: Images from Google are all public domain
Google images are always lower quality
Google only allows images in Google Slides
Google shows other people's images; it does not own them
q.why: Google Images is a search engine; the pictures belong to their creators.

q.q: Ronan makes a realistic AI image of the Erne in flood for his slide. What should he do?
o: Give it a CC BY licence and his name
Label it as AI-generated and list the tool
Use it without any caption at all
Say it is a photo he took himself
q.why: A realistic AI image could be mistaken for a real photo, so it must be clearly labelled.

q.q: Which use of generative AI in a presentation is dishonest?
o: Labelling an AI picture as an illustration
Listing the AI tool on the sources slide
Checking an AI image for mistakes
Showing an AI image as a real event photo
q.why: Passing off an AI image as a real photo misleads the audience.

q.q: Which chart is best for showing how something changes over time?
q.why: A line chart shows a trend over time.

q.q: Which chart best shows how 120 pupils split their votes between three trip choices?
q.why: Shares of a whole group suit a pie chart.

q.q: Which SmartArt type suits the stages of the water cycle?
q.why: A repeating loop is shown with a cycle diagram.

q.q: Which SmartArt type suits a chart of who is in charge of whom in a school?
q.why: Levels of responsibility are shown with a hierarchy.

q.q: How can you turn an existing bulleted list into a diagram?
q.why: Convert to SmartArt on the Home tab changes a list into a SmartArt diagram.

q.q: What opens when you insert a chart in PowerPoint?
o: A web browser to search for data
A small spreadsheet to type the data in
q.why: A data sheet opens and the chart updates as you type.

q.q: Seán uses a line chart to compare the number of pupils in 8A, 8B and 8C. Why is this a poor choice?
o: Line charts need at least ten classes
Line charts cannot show whole numbers
A line suggests a trend between separate classes
q.why: Separate categories should be compared with a column or bar chart.

q.q: Which piece of information is best shown as a table?
o: Prices and features of three phones
Temperature each day for a month
q.why: Comparing several items across several headings suits a table.

q.q: What is a transition?
o: An effect played when moving between slides
An effect on one object within a slide
A link that jumps to a web page
A note that only the speaker can see
q.why: Transitions happen between slides; animations act on objects on a slide.

q.q: Which type of animation draws attention to something already on the slide?
q.why: Emphasis effects, shown with yellow stars, highlight existing objects.

q.q: Exit animation effects are shown in PowerPoint with which colour star?
q.why: Entrance is green, emphasis yellow and exit red.

q.q: An animation set to With Previous will…
o: Play only when the slide ends
Start after the one before finishes
Wait for the presenter to click
Start at the same time as the one before
q.why: With Previous starts together with the previous effect; After Previous waits for it to finish.

q.q: Which setting makes a slide move on by itself after a set time?
q.why: On the Transitions tab, ticking After with a time advances the slide automatically.

q.q: Niamh wants each picture to appear with its bullet point without an extra click. Which Start option should the pictures use?
o: After Previous with a 5 second delay
q.why: With Previous plays the picture at the same moment as its bullet point.

q.q: Where can you see and drag to reorder every animation on a slide?
q.why: The Animation Pane lists every effect on the slide in order.

q.q: Which is the most sensible use of effects in a class presentation?
o: A different flashy transition per slide
A whoosh sound on every click
One subtle transition on every slide
q.why: Subtle, consistent effects support the message instead of distracting from it.

q.q: Apart from being distracting, why else should fast flashing effects be avoided?
o: They can be uncomfortable for some viewers
q.why: Flashing or spinning movement can affect people with vestibular conditions or photosensitive epilepsy.

q.q: Which shortcut opens the Insert Link box?
q.why: Ctrl + K inserts a hyperlink.

q.q: What is a non-linear presentation?
o: One that has only a single slide
One with no pictures or charts
One where users choose the next slide by clicking
One that always runs in slide number order
q.why: Non-linear presentations use links and buttons so users choose their own route.

q.q: Where are action buttons such as Home and Back found?
q.why: Action buttons are at the bottom of the Insert > Shapes menu.

q.q: When do hyperlinks on a slide work with a normal click?
q.why: Links work in Slide Show view; in Normal view you need Ctrl + click.

q.q: In a quiz, the right answer should link to the Correct slide. Where should the two wrong answers link?
o: To the last slide of the show
To the Correct slide as well
q.why: Wrong answers go to a Try again slide that has a button back to the question.

q.q: The Try again slide is slide 7 and the question is slide 3. Why is a Previous Slide button a mistake?
o: It goes to slide 6, not slide 3
It only works in kiosk mode
q.why: Previous Slide goes to the slide numbered one lower; link to slide 3 or use Last Slide Viewed.

q.q: How do you set a presentation to run as a kiosk?
o: Slide Show > Set Up Slide Show
q.why: Choose Browsed at a kiosk (full screen) in Set Up Slide Show.

q.q: In kiosk mode, what happens when a visitor clicks an empty part of a slide?
o: It moves to the next slide
Nothing, the slide does not advance
q.why: In kiosk mode only links, buttons and timings move the show on.

q.q: Which feature in Microsoft 365 automatically makes a menu slide of clickable thumbnails?
q.why: Insert > Zoom > Summary Zoom creates a clickable menu slide.

q.q: What is alt text?
o: Text that appears when you hover over a link
A description of an image read by a screen reader
Text hidden in the speaker notes
A second font used for titles
q.why: Alt text describes an image so screen reader users know what it shows.

q.q: Which is the best alt text for a photo of Enniskillen Castle's Watergate?
o: The Watergate of Enniskillen Castle beside the river
q.why: Good alt text briefly says what the image shows.

q.q: Roughly how many men are colour blind?
q.why: About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women are colour blind.

q.q: A quiz shows right answers in green and wrong answers in red, and nothing else. How should it be fixed?
o: Add a tick or cross as well as the colour
Add a transition to each answer
Use a darker shade of red
q.why: Never use colour alone to show meaning: add a symbol or word.

q.q: Where is the Accessibility Checker?
o: Slide Show > Set Up Slide Show
q.why: Review > Check Accessibility lists errors, warnings and tips.

q.q: What does WCAG stand for?
q.why: WCAG are the international accessibility guidelines from the W3C.

q.q: What are the four WCAG principles?
q.why: Remember POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

q.q: WCAG level AA asks for a contrast ratio of at least what for normal-sized text?
q.why: Normal text needs at least 4.5 : 1; large text needs at least 3 : 1.

q.q: Why should every slide have its own unique title?
o: Titles make the slides load faster
PowerPoint will not save untitled slides
Screen reader users move between slides by title
q.why: Unique titles let screen reader users find and jump to slides.

q.q: Which job can the Accessibility Checker not do for you?
o: Check whether your alt text is accurate
Find pictures with no alt text
q.why: It can spot missing alt text but cannot judge whether a description is correct.

q.q: Who can see the speaker notes in Presenter View?
q.why: Presenter View shows the notes on the presenter's screen only.

q.q: What does Presenter View show on the presenter's screen?
o: The Slide Master and its layouts
Only the current slide, full screen
Current slide, next slide, notes and a timer
q.why: The audience sees only the slide; the presenter also sees notes, the next slide and a timer.

q.q: A talk has 12 slides at about 30 seconds each. How long does it last?
q.why: 12 × 30 = 360 seconds, which is 6 minutes.

q.q: Saoirse's 12-slide talk is 6 minutes but the limit is 5. About how many seconds per slide must she aim for?
q.why: 5 minutes = 300 seconds, and 300 ÷ 12 = 25 seconds per slide.

q.q: A talk has 15 slides at about 40 seconds each. How long does it last?
q.why: 15 × 40 = 600 seconds = 10 minutes.

q.q: Which key shows a black screen during a slide show?
q.why: B blacks the screen and pressing it again returns; W gives a white screen.

q.q: Which is the best advice for writing speaker notes?
o: Copy the slide text into the notes exactly
Put the notes on the slide itself
Leave the notes empty to sound natural
Write short prompts, not a script to read
q.why: Prompts remind you what to say while keeping eye contact.

q.q: Why should a presenter not read the slides aloud word for word?
o: It makes the slide text disappear
PowerPoint will stop the slide show
The audience reads faster and gets bored
It breaks the Rehearse Timings tool
q.why: The slides show key points; the speaker should explain them, not read them.

q.q: What are success criteria?
o: The final mark the teacher awards
A checklist of what good work must do
q.why: Success criteria set out what the work should achieve, usually agreed before starting.

q.q: Which success criterion is the easiest to check?
o: All body text is at least 24 point
There is not too much writing
q.why: A specific, measurable criterion can be checked with a clear yes or no.

q.q: What does two stars and a wish mean in peer feedback?
o: Two strengths and one thing to improve
Two slides to delete and one to add
Two marks out of a possible three
q.why: Two things done well plus one specific improvement.

q.q: Which piece of peer feedback is the most helpful?
o: Add alt text to the photo on slide 5
Your slides were a bit boring
I liked it but it was long
q.why: It is specific and tells the presenter exactly what to change.

q.q: What should a good evaluation give for each success criterion?
o: A list of the slide titles used
Only the things that went well
A judgement, evidence and a specific improvement
The software version that was used
q.why: Judge it, back it up with evidence, then say exactly how to improve.

q.q: What does usability mean?
o: How many slides a presentation has
How old the target audience is
How large the saved file is
How easy a product is for its users to use
q.why: Usability is about ease of use; improving it is the aim of refining.

q.q: Testers get stuck on Cara's Try again slide. What is the best refinement?
o: Delete the Try again slide entirely
Add a Back button and test again
q.why: Fix the problem the users found, then re-test with users to check it worked.

q.q: Why is "I wouldn't change anything" a weak evaluation?
o: It is too long for an evaluation
Every piece of work can be improved
q.why: Saying how to improve shows you understand the criteria.

q.q: Why is peer feedback useful when evaluating?
o: It means the teacher does not mark it
Classmates notice problems the author misses
Peers can change the slides for you
It replaces the need for success criteria
q.why: Peers see the work as an audience does and can spot problems you cannot.
